# CLEAR-100 rules in full

43 rules. Severity `error` blocks a ship. `warn` needs a reason to keep. `review` is a prompt to look, not a verdict.

## Plain

### P1 One sentence, one length limit

`warn`, weight 2, detector `sentence_length`

**Why.** Past about 25 words a reader has to hold too much in memory to finish the thought. Aerospace maintenance manuals cap procedures at 20 words for the same reason.

**Fix.** Split at the conjunction. Two short sentences always beat one long one.

```text
BAD:  Because the pipeline retries on failure and the retry budget is shared across every worker in the pool, a single slow endpoint can starve unrelated jobs that would otherwise have completed.
GOOD: The retry budget is shared across every worker. So one slow endpoint can starve unrelated jobs.
```

### P2 One instruction per sentence

`warn`, weight 2, detector `regex`

**Why.** A reader following steps does one thing at a time. Two instructions in one sentence get half done.

**Fix.** Make it a numbered list. One step per line.

```text
BAD:  First install the CLI and then run the migration and check the output.
GOOD: 1. Install the CLI.
2. Run the migration.
3. Check the output.
```

### P3 No semicolons in reader-facing prose

`review`, weight 1, detector `regex`

**Why.** A semicolon is a sentence break that a hurried reader misses. It also signals two ideas fused for no reason.

**Fix.** Use a period. Start a new sentence.

```text
BAD:  The job failed twice; the third run succeeded.
GOOD: The job failed twice. The third run succeeded.
```

### P4 Active voice for anything a person does

`warn`, weight 2, detector `regex`

**Why.** Passive voice hides who acts. A reader who cannot tell who does the thing cannot do the thing.

**Fix.** Put the actor first. Subject, verb, object.

```text
BAD:  The config is validated by the loader before the run is started.
GOOD: The loader validates the config before it starts the run.
```

### P5 Use the short word

`warn`, weight 1, detector `substitution`

**Why.** Long formal words cost the reader time and buy nothing. Plain-language research finds high-literacy readers prefer the short word too, because they finish faster.

**Fix.** Swap in the plain alternative from the substitution table.

```text
BAD:  We utilize the gateway to facilitate the transfer prior to commencement.
GOOD: We use the gateway to move the data before we start.
```

### P6 Gloss jargon on first use

`warn`, weight 3, detector `jargon_gloss`

**Why.** A term of art is a wall. One six-word gloss keeps the non-specialist reading instead of leaving.

**Fix.** On first use, add a short plain gloss in parentheses or in the next clause. Never gloss twice.

```text
BAD:  The handler is idempotent, so the queue can redeliver freely.
GOOD: The handler is idempotent (running it twice changes nothing), so the queue can redeliver freely.
```

### P7 Expand an acronym on first use

`warn`, weight 2, detector `acronym_gloss`

**Why.** An unexpanded acronym reads as insider shorthand and stops everyone else.

**Fix.** Write it out once, then use the short form. Skip this only for acronyms your whole audience already owns.

```text
BAD:  Route the RAG call through the MCP layer.
GOOD: Route the retrieval call through MCP (Model Context Protocol, the standard way tools plug into a model).
```

### P8 Hold the reading grade

`warn`, weight 3, detector `grade_level`

**Why.** Most adults read comfortably at about grade 8. Text above the profile target loses readers who could have used it.

**Fix.** Shorten sentences first, then swap long words. Those two moves carry almost all of the score.

### P9 Cap noun stacks

`review`, weight 1, detector `noun_cluster`

**Why.** Four nouns in a row can be parsed several ways. The reader guesses, and sometimes guesses wrong.

**Fix.** Break the stack with a preposition.

```text
BAD:  customer data retention policy exception process
GOOD: the process for an exception to the policy on keeping customer data
```

### P10 Unbury the verb

`warn`, weight 2, detector `regex`

**Why.** A verb turned into a noun needs a weak helper verb to stand up. The sentence gets longer and vaguer.

**Fix.** Use the verb itself.

```text
BAD:  The team made a decision to provide an explanation.
GOOD: The team decided to explain.
```

### P11 Keep contractions

`review`, weight 1, detector `stiffness`

**Why.** Controlled technical English bans contractions, which is correct for a mechanic on a runway and wrong for everyone else. Expanded forms everywhere read stiff and formal, and formal reads like a machine.

**Fix.** Use don't, can't, it's, you're where a person would say them out loud.

```text
BAD:  It is not possible to retry. You will need to restart the run.
GOOD: You can't retry. Restart the run.
```

### P12 Numerals and units, not adjectives

`review`, weight 1, detector `regex`

**Why.** A vague quantity is unfalsifiable and forgettable. A number is neither.

**Fix.** Replace with the count, the percent, or the duration.

```text
BAD:  We cut latency significantly across many endpoints.
GOOD: We cut p95 latency from 840ms to 190ms across 14 endpoints.
```

## Human

### H1 No slop vocabulary

`error`, weight 3, detector `slop_words`

**Why.** These words spiked in frequency after 2022 and now function as a signature. Readers who use models daily spot them fast, and they discount the whole piece.

**Fix.** Say the specific thing the word was standing in for. If nothing specific is behind it, delete the sentence.

```text
BAD:  This robust framework unlocks a seamless developer experience.
GOOD: The framework retries failed jobs on its own, so nobody gets paged at 3am.
```

### H2 No slop phrases

`error`, weight 3, detector `slop_phrases`

**Why.** Whole clauses that carry no information and appear in every model output.

**Fix.** Delete. If the sentence dies without the phrase, the sentence was the phrase.

```text
BAD:  In today's fast-paced digital landscape, it's important to note that AI is a game-changer.
GOOD: AI cut our support queue by 40% in six weeks. Here is what broke on the way.
```

### H3 No canned sentence openers

`warn`, weight 2, detector `banned_openers`

**Why.** Furthermore, Moreover, Additionally and their family are transition words a model reaches for when it has nothing new to add.

**Fix.** Start with the subject of the new fact. Or cut the sentence.

```text
BAD:  Furthermore, the cache also improves latency.
GOOD: The cache also cut latency by half.
```

### H4 No em-dash, no en-dash used as one

`error`, weight 3, detector `dashes`

**Why.** The strongest surviving punctuation tell. Humans reach for a comma, a period, or parentheses. Models reach for the long dash.

**Fix.** Use a period and a new sentence, a comma, a spaced hyphen, or parentheses.

### H5 Straight quotes and apostrophes

`warn`, weight 1, detector `smart_punctuation`

**Why.** Curly quotes arrive when text is pasted out of a model or a word processor. They are a provenance tell and they break code blocks.

**Fix.** Use straight quotes.

### H6 No negative parallelism

`error`, weight 3, detector `regex`

**Why.** The single most recognizable model rhythm. It manufactures a contrast with an assumption nobody made.

**Fix.** State the claim once, directly.

```text
BAD:  This isn't just a linter. It's a standard.
GOOD: This is a standard with a linter attached.
```

### H7 Break the rule of three

`warn`, weight 2, detector `rule_of_three`

**Why.** Three rhythmic items in a row is a cadence, not an argument. Repeated across a piece it is unmistakable.

**Fix.** Use two items, or four, or make it a real list with real content per item.

```text
BAD:  It is fast, reliable, and scalable.
GOOD: It answers in under 200ms. It has not dropped a job in 40 days.
```

### H8 Say is, not serves as

`warn`, weight 2, detector `regex`

**Why.** Models avoid plain copulas. Measured use of is and are dropped over ten percent in academic text after 2022.

**Fix.** Use is, are, or has.

```text
BAD:  The repo serves as a reference implementation and boasts 400 stars.
GOOD: The repo is a reference implementation. It has 400 stars.
```

### H9 No promotional adjectives

`warn`, weight 2, detector `promo_words`

**Why.** Vibrant, rich, profound, groundbreaking. Travel-brochure vocabulary applied to software.

**Fix.** Replace with the measurement or the mechanism.

```text
BAD:  A vibrant ecosystem with a rich set of groundbreaking features.
GOOD: Nine plugins, six written by people I have never met.
```

### H10 No trailing -ing analysis

`warn`, weight 2, detector `regex`

**Why.** Clauses like highlighting the importance of and ensuring seamless integration attach commentary that says nothing.

**Fix.** Cut the clause. If the point matters, make it its own sentence with a fact in it.

```text
BAD:  The team shipped the parser, highlighting the importance of clear specs.
GOOD: The team shipped the parser. The spec rewrite took longer than the parser did.
```

### H11 Name the source or drop the claim

`warn`, weight 2, detector `regex`

**Why.** Vague attribution turns one source into a consensus, or invents one. It is also how hallucinated citations enter a draft.

**Fix.** Name the study, the person, and the year, with a link. Or write it as your own claim.

```text
BAD:  Studies show plain language improves comprehension.
GOOD: GOV.UK found high-literacy readers prefer plain English because they finish faster.
```

### H12 No assistant voice

`error`, weight 3, detector `assistant_voice`

**Why.** Great question, I hope this helps, let me know if you need anything else. Chat-window residue leaking into published text.

**Fix.** Delete. Published text has no counterparty to be polite to.

```text
BAD:  Great question! I hope this helps. Feel free to reach out.
GOOD: 
```

### H13 Vary sentence length

`warn`, weight 2, detector `uniformity`

**Why.** Human prose has jagged rhythm. Model prose settles into a narrow band of 15 to 20 words per sentence and stays there.

**Fix.** Put a four-word sentence next to a 28-word one. Read it out loud.

### H14 No model self-reference

`error`, weight 3, detector `regex`

**Why.** Nothing published should reference the tool that drafted it.

**Fix.** Delete the sentence and answer the question, or say the fact is unverified and why.

```text
BAD:  As an AI, I don't have access to real-time data.
GOOD: The last figure I verified was from 2026-08-10.
```

### H15 Do not announce that you are stopping

`warn`, weight 2, detector `regex`

**Why.** A closing label adds a sentence and no information. The reader can see the page ending.

**Fix.** Stop. Or end on the strongest concrete fact.

```text
BAD:  In conclusion, plain language wins.
GOOD: Six of the seven readers finished the plain version. Two finished the original.
```

### H16 No hedge stacking

`review`, weight 1, detector `regex`

**Why.** Hedges buy the writer safety and cost the reader confidence.

**Fix.** Say the thing, or say the exact limit of what you know.

```text
BAD:  It's worth noting that results may vary in some cases.
GOOD: This held on 14 of 16 runs. Both failures were on cold starts.
```

## Structured

### S1 Three parallel items become a list

`warn`, weight 2, detector `list_candidate`

**Why.** Parallel items buried in a sentence are read once and remembered never. As a list they survive scanning.

**Fix.** Break the sentence into a bulleted list, one item per line.

```text
BAD:  The checker scores plainness, humanity, structure, and density.
GOOD: The checker scores four things:
- Plain
- Human
- Structured
- Dense
```

### S2 Sequences become numbered steps

`warn`, weight 2, detector `step_candidate`

**Why.** A reader executing a sequence needs to find their place again after looking away.

**Fix.** Numbered list. One action per number.

```text
BAD:  Clone the repo, then install the skill, then restart the agent.
GOOD: 1. Clone the repo.
2. Install the skill.
3. Restart the agent.
```

### S3 Comparisons become a table

`review`, weight 1, detector `table_candidate`

**Why.** Two or more options across two or more attributes is a grid. Prose forces the reader to build the grid in their head.

**Fix.** Write the table.

```text
BAD:  Option A is cheaper but slower, while option B costs more and finishes faster, and option C is mid on both.
GOOD: | Option | Cost | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| A | low | slow |
| B | high | fast |
| C | mid | mid |
```

### S4 Cap paragraph length

`warn`, weight 2, detector `paragraph_length`

**Why.** A block over four sentences reads as a wall and gets skipped on a phone.

**Fix.** Break at the topic shift. Blank line between paragraphs.

### S5 One topic per paragraph

`review`, weight 1, detector `paragraph_topics`

**Why.** Two topics in one block means neither gets a heading, and neither is findable later.

**Fix.** Split. Give each its own paragraph, and a heading if it earns one.

### S6 Heading levels do not skip

`warn`, weight 1, detector `heading_hygiene`

**Why.** A skipped level breaks screen readers and the document outline.

**Fix.** Go h2 then h3. Never h2 then h4.

```text
BAD:  ## Setup
#### Install
GOOD: ## Setup
### Install
```

### S7 Sentence-case headings

`warn`, weight 1, detector `heading_case`

**Why.** Title Case On Every Heading is a formatting tell and it slows scanning.

**Fix.** Capitalize the first word and proper nouns only.

```text
BAD:  ## How To Install The Skill
GOOD: ## How to install the skill
```

### S8 Bold is for one thing per screen

`warn`, weight 2, detector `bold_density`

**Why.** When everything is bold nothing is. Bold spam is one of the clearest model formatting habits.

**Fix.** Keep bold under five percent of words. One idea per section.

### S9 No emoji as structure

`warn`, weight 2, detector `emoji_structure`

**Why.** Emoji bullets and emoji headings are decoration standing in for a real hierarchy.

**Fix.** Use real bullets and real headings.

### S10 Long pieces lead with the answer

`warn`, weight 2, detector `tldr_missing`

**Why.** Most readers decide in the first screen. Burying the conclusion costs you the ones who would have acted on it.

**Fix.** Open with the conclusion in one to three lines, then the detail.

## Dense

### D1 The delete test

`warn`, weight 3, detector `density`

**Why.** The slop research finds low information density is what readers actually react to, more than any single word. A sentence with no number, name, mechanism, or consequence is filler.

**Fix.** Delete it, or replace it with the fact it was gesturing at.

```text
BAD:  Automation has become an increasingly important part of modern engineering practice.
GOOD: Four of our six deploy steps now run without a human. The other two need a card on file.
```

### D2 No restatement

`warn`, weight 2, detector `restatement`

**Why.** Consecutive sentences that share most of their content words are one sentence written twice.

**Fix.** Keep the sharper one. Delete the other.

```text
BAD:  The cache reduced latency. Latency was reduced by the cache.
GOOD: The cache cut p95 latency from 840ms to 190ms.
```

### D3 No throat-clearing opener

`error`, weight 3, detector `opener_density`

**Why.** The first sentence is the only one every reader reads. Spending it on setup is the most expensive mistake in the piece.

**Fix.** Lead with the number, the name, or the claim.

```text
BAD:  Writing clearly is something many teams struggle with these days.
GOOD: Our docs scored grade 14. Support tickets dropped 31% after we got them to grade 8.
```

### D4 The horoscope test

`review`, weight 2, detector `horoscope`

**Why.** If a paragraph could appear in any article on any adjacent topic, it belongs to none of them.

**Fix.** Anchor it to your specific case: a name, a date, a number, a file, a failure.

### D5 No filler intensifiers

`warn`, weight 1, detector `filler`

**Why.** Very, really, quite, basically, simply, actually. Each one weakens the word it is trying to strengthen.

**Fix.** Delete the intensifier. If the claim now looks weak, the claim was weak.

```text
BAD:  This is really quite simply the best approach.
GOOD: This is the approach we kept after trying three.
```
